title: High school bands and Al Hirt
summary: Steinau talks about strong white high school bands, Al Hirt as a product of that period, and the lack of jazz there.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Uh, except I, I don't remember if the Jefferson City Buzzards and those marching groups sometimes used them or not. I think they had black brass bands. I remember black brass bands. I don't remember white brass bands. But then, of course, there were, there were a lot of, there was a lot of interest in the high schools, in the, in the white high schools, in, uh, in band music. Yeah. And the high school I went to was, had, the bands have made high state ratings for many years. Mm-hmm. And, uh, in fact, what's his name, uh, Al Hurt was one of, was one of the products of that particular period. Uh, although he finished when I was coming in, as I remember. Mm-hmm. And I never heard him until, I guess it must have been the fifties, and not much then. Yeah, I don't think people were paying much attention to him, maybe.
He was on the road without, uh, with, uh, Horace Hite after a while.
Came back to town, or something. Yeah. And he'd gone off even, I find, at the Music Conservatory.

Oh, really? Yeah. I know the, uh, I think it was Michael Caparo was the band director at Fort Che for a number of years, and he apparently produced some good musicians at various times. Mm-hmm. But, uh, no one played what anyone would call jazz, or at least what I identified as it,
or even thought of it. Probably not even any approaching a big band swing arrangement, whether they had solos or not.
